newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - The yankees are coming.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - The yankees are coming.

text.p: While currency, credit and macro-economic concerns may be paralysing local debt markets, Asian issuers continue to blaze a trail to the United States.
U.S. rates remain so low, with little prospect of rising, that Asian issuers can afford to pay a premium and still lock in longer tenors and lower rates than they could get in Asia.
"The Asian market is taking a bit of a breather," one investment banker said.
But the same cannot be said of the yankee market, which is being swamped by East Asian borrowers.
Korean Electric Power Co (KEPCO) plans a US$200 million 30-year yankee with a put option at year seven.
Last week, Kepco raised US$500 million through a 364-day floating-rate note (FRN) arranged by SBC Warburg at 15 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR).
Its latest move follows issues or planned issues from the region's blue-chip banks and corporates, whose names are now well-known both in the region and in other markets.
"These are pretty good underlying credits. They're not exactly unknown names," said one Hong Kong syndicate head.
Pusan Bank is considering a US$100 million yankee or global bond.
Also waiting in the wings to enter the U.S. dollar market is TATA Electric Co, which has mandated Chase to arrange a eurobond with 144a placement for up to US$300 million.
Industrial Development Bank of India is considering a US$300 million yankee with a 10-year tenor, bankers said.
In Thailand, Bank of Ayudhya has mandated JP Morgan to arrange a yankee. The bank said in May JP Morgan would arrange a US$150 million issue of subordinated bonds.
One of those tipped as looking at the yankee or global market is also Industrial and Finance Corp of Thailand (IFCT), an early victim of Thai credit concern.
IFCT pulled a step-up US$150 million FRN in June after being downgraded by a domestic and an international rating agency.
Bankers said it appeared that Lehman Brothers had won the mandate to bring IFCT to the yankee market.
Bankers said U.S. investors liked the yield pickup on Asian debt and were more familiar with the region and the credits.
"Credit-buyers are pretty clued up," said a banker with a U.S. investment bank. "The risk is reflected in the yield."
The shift to U.S. debt issues is taking its toll on regional debt arrangers, banks said.
"It's anathema to us in the Hong Kong debt market," said one banker active in the Hong Kong dollar market, sidelined because of interest rate volatility and the trend towards the yankee market.
In other news, Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) surprised the market by cutting cash rates by 0.5 percentage points.
"Just about everybody has been expecting a rate cut in the very short-term, and the RBA has come through," said Michael Blythe, senior economist with Commonwealth Bank of Australia.

In Hong Kong, Paliburg Holdings Ltd, part of a consortium that paid HK$5.5 billion for a section of land in Hong Kong's last colonial land auction, is seeking HK$3.3 billion through a syndicated loan, bankers said.
